title: Best Resistance Bands UK
short: Loop, tube and superband resistance bands compared by durability, resistance range and accessories, from budget sets to premium heavy-duty bands.
intro: A resistance band's build quality determines whether it lasts for years or snaps mid-workout, and the right style depends on what you're training. This guide compares bands tested by Tom's Guide's fitness editor across bicep curls, assisted pull-ups, lateral walks and push-ups.

products.name: Resistance Bands Set

guide.q: Loop bands, tube bands or superbands: what's the difference?
guide.a: Loop bands (mini bands), like the Perform Better here, are small closed loops best for glute and lower-body activation. Tube bands have handles on each end, suited to upper-body moves like curls and presses. Superbands are large, thick loops used for assisted pull-ups or added resistance on squats and deadlifts.

guide.q: What resistance level should I start with?
guide.a: Beginners should start with lighter, thinner bands and build up as strength improves. As a rule of thumb, the last few reps of any exercise should feel genuinely challenging without breaking form; if a band feels easy throughout, it's time to size up.

guide.q: Do I need a latex-free band?
guide.a: If you have a latex allergy or sensitive skin, look specifically for non-latex bands like TheraBand's synthetic rubber range here, since most resistance bands are made from natural rubber latex by default.

guide.q: Are resistance bands a genuine substitute for weights?
guide.a: They work differently rather than as a direct substitute: bands keep muscles under constant tension throughout a movement, which builds strength effectively, and they're particularly useful for injury rehab or building up before returning to free weights. Many lifters use both together rather than choosing one exclusively.
